concerns.owns: The one ordered destination list feeding every navigation surface. The only surface meeting the 44px touch floor by construction. **NORTH1 (2026-07-17) gave it a third consumer and its first EXPORT.** Home's North Star puts four of the house's rooms on the counter as doors, which makes Home a navigation surface — and this row's own rule is that ONE ordered list is the single source of truth for EVERY navigation surface. Home therefore reads its doors from here through the new `roomsByHref(hrefs)` helper rather than keeping a second list; a private copy would have been a second owner of every room's href, label and glyph, and the first rename would have silently forked the house. `roomsByHref` throws on an unknown href rather than rendering a door to nowhere. **NORTH3 (2026-07-17) retired that sentence, and Home now owns nothing here at all.** This row used to read: *"Home owns only the SENTENCE under each door, which is Home's furniture and not the walls."* Those four sentences (`DOOR_LINES` — "Plan your meals with ease", "Discover recipes and inspiration", "See what you have at home", "Your list and reminders") were the last strings on Home with **no owner and no source**: not facts about the household, not facts from a canonical owner, and not anything a person standing in their own hall has ever needed to be told. NORTH1 § 5.7 had already deleted the render's "Nourishing food. Happy home." from this room as *a marketing line inside the product* — and then kept four more of exactly that on the doors. A door carries a NAME and a HANDLE; it does not carry a paragraph explaining the room behind it. **Home now takes the href, the label and the glyph from this owner and adds nothing**, which is a stricter reading of this row's own rule, not a looser one. **The walls themselves are untouched** (Blueprint § 14): the canonical BottomNav is still the sole primary navigation at every size, still holds all eight destinations, and the render's left sidebar is refused — UX1 retired the DesktopSidebar and NORTH1 did not revive it.

exemptions.why: No page imports the nav directly — `WorkspaceHeader` mounts it. Home is the one page that imports this module, and it imports the LIST rather than the nav: it renders four rooms as doors on its counter and reads their hrefs, labels and glyphs from here. Three importers is the correct number, not a high one — the alternative was a fourth copy of the house's room list.

THA in its own hand. The signature voice admitted by **UIA §8 (amended by UXHOME1)**, which replaced *"two voices only; no third typeface, ever"* with three named families and a hard boundary: the signature is for **emotionally significant branded moments only** and is forbidden in all functional UI — buttons, forms, navigation, tables, cards, modals, planner, shopping. `.text-signature` is the ONE entry point: no `font-signature` Tailwind utility exists, deliberately (tailwind.config.ts carries the comment saying so), because a utility would be a one-token door into the third typeface from any surface in the product. **The webfont is not loaded in production** — the token resolves, but the only surface that fetches Caveat is the dev-only prototype below, so no household downloads a font for a page they cannot reach. **Permitted surfaces — exactly three, and none is a household surface:** `pages/dev/arrival-experience.tsx` (`/dev/arrival`, ARRIVAL1), `pages/dev/arrival-a-welcome.tsx` (`/dev/arrival-a-welcome`, EXP2 exploration Prototype A — admitted by a governed edit, 2026-07-15, for the same emotionally significant moment: the arrival greeting, and nothing else), and `pages/dev/arrival-s1-quiet.tsx` (`/dev/arrival-s1-quiet`, EXP3 synthesis candidate S1 — admitted by this governed edit, 2026-07-15, carrying Prototype A's greeting forward into the synthesis: the same one moment, the arrival greeting, and nothing else). All three are `import.meta.env.DEV` only; the chunks are dropped from the production bundle, verified in the build. This surface replaced UXHOME1's `home-arrival-prototype.tsx`, which was discarded by ARRIVAL1 — the signature voice now says its one word ("Welcome home") inside an *arrival* rather than over an animated Home page. A second surface does not follow from the first: §8 requires a further governed decision, per surface. The failure mode this row exists to catch is not ugliness but **familiarity** — the moment the signature becomes an ordinary UI font, the identity it was admitted to carry is gone and using it more cannot bring it back.

**NORTH3 (2026-07-17) — `.text-signature` moved from `@layer utilities` to `@layer components`, and that CHANGED ITS CONTRACT.** The role was declared inside `@layer utilities` at index.css:593 — *after* `@tailwind utilities` at line 10. A role and a Tailwind utility are both single-class selectors, so specificity ties and **source order decided**: the role won every contest, always, and any utility aimed at it was dead on arrival. It was not a starting point; it was a cage, and it was silent about it. **Home's own signature carried `leading-[1.02]` and measured 1.15** — this role's own line-height, to the decimal. The same defect had already killed NORTH2's `title-page font-normal` on the salutation beside it (see `type-roles` below). The role now sits in `components`, which is the relationship Tailwind's layer order (base → components → utilities) exists to express: **components name a thing, utilities adjust it.** This admits no new pattern under UIA § 17 — it applies the pattern the layer system already had to the one block that had opted out of it. `.text-signature` remains the ONE entry point to the third voice and its permitted-surface rule is **byte-unchanged**: moving a role's layer changes what a permitted surface may ADJUST, never who may USE it.

exemptions.why: Not an exemption from the owner — an exemption from USING it, and it is now the rule rather than the gap. **The ADOPT ruling (Colin Clapson, 2026-07-17, recorded by ODL2) was EXECUTED by NORTH1 on the same day**: `/home` is the one permitted surface, and the one thing on it in the signature voice is the household's own name in the greeting — Home's single ornament (Blueprint § 12.1), and data-borne. Caveat is loaded from the `@import` in `client/src/index.css`, which is the first time a household downloads it. The rarity is the whole point: the voice is never a button, a label, a status, or a value a household reads in order to act. A second permitted surface is a governed decision, named here one at a time, and there is no second one.

concerns.owns:
**The orchard environment asset — the image itself.** This is the named canonical owner **THA_EXPERIENCE_BLUEPRINT.md § 6.1 requires** ("one canonical environment, one owner, one season"), and naming it here **closes Blueprint § 18 open item 1** (ODL2, 2026-07-17), which had blocked exposure levels from becoming governed tokens. This row stood since CONV1-P3 under the name "Orchard exposure" while owning the asset and expressly disclaiming the scale in its own text — so the asset read as unowned and the scale read as owned, when the truth was exactly the reverse. ODL2 renamed it to what it owns; the E0–E3 scale now has its own row below. It is an ARRIVAL surface and nothing else: /auth and /onboarding (through orchard-shell.tsx) and the unauthenticated marketing landing (home-page.tsx). Blueprint § 6.2 rule 3 expressly permits arrival to stand at E3. A ROOM may never mount it: rooms receive the orchard as governed E0–E3 exposure values (§ 6.2), never as this component. **The raw-value defect is FIXED (ODL2, 2026-07-17).** The component hardcoded `opacity: 0.90` — a raw value in a surface, which UIA § 16 calls a defect. It now resolves `--orchard-exposure-e3`, whose value IS 0.90, so arrival renders exactly as it did; what changed is that the number has one home and a name. This component is the exposure scale's first consumer, which is what made admitting the scale lawful rather than authoring a foundation to adopt later.

**NORTH1 (2026-07-17) — a SECOND SHAPE, on the same owner, and a correction to this row's own text.** This row said "a ROOM may never mount it". That sentence was right about the SHAPE and wrong about the ASSET, and Home's E3 is what proved the difference. What Blueprint § 6.1 forbids is the wallpaper — `fixed inset-0` behind every room, uniformly, at one strength — which is what CONV1 BEH-7 retired and what this row was written to keep retired. It does not forbid Home the view its own exposure level is DEFINED by (§ 6.2: E3, "the orchard visible as itself, generously", Home only). Read literally, the old sentence made E3 unbuildable and left the scale with three usable levels and a fourth nobody could ever reach. So the open view was added to THIS FILE rather than to a second component: a second file rendering `/orchard-bg.webp` would be a second owner of one visual concern, which UIA § 17 forbids and which this row exists to prevent. The file now exports two shapes and owns the asset in both: `OrchardBackdrop` (arrival's full-bleed E3 — /auth, /onboarding via orchard-shell.tsx, and the unauthenticated landing, all unchanged) and `OrchardOpenView` (Home's E3 — a composed, bounded window that dissolves before the household's name and before the counter, so no type on the page ever has the image behind it). **Permitted surfaces are now: arrival, and `/home`. Nothing else. Any other room mounting either shape is still the wallpaper, and is still forbidden.**

**NORTH2 (2026-07-17) — the asset is GRADED, and the grade is in the FILE.** The orchard was pale; at E3 behind a warm room it read as a haze — a background image, not a view. It is now graded (saturation 1.28, contrast 1.06) and baked into `/orchard-bg.webp` itself: 56,986 → **51,722 bytes**, so PX1-W3's performance budget is IMPROVED, not spent. It was a CSS `filter:` on this owner's three shapes first, and that was a latent SECOND ORCHARD — see the openMigration below. Grading the asset makes Blueprint §6.1's one orchard true BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by discipline, costs no runtime filter, and will not double-grade the real photograph when it lands. It adds no second light and moves no sun: a grade changes how a negative is PRINTED, never where the morning comes from. **The grade is a ceiling, not a fix** — NORTH2 established that this asset is a pale watercolour of a MEADOW (rolling hills, a path, a few generic horizon trees; no apple trees, no rows, no blossom, no fruit). All four copies in the repository are byte-identical (md5 332f82…) and the shipped webp was visually indistinguishable from the 2MB PNG it came from, so **there was never a richer version to restore**. concerns.owns:
**The § 4 depth and light vocabulary, as values** — the ground plane (materiality), warm shadow (depth), one light and the penumbra (warm light), plus the radius ladder that governs what rests on what. **The law is UIA § 4** (amended by ODL2); this file is the values' one home (§ 16). One row, not three: EXP4's central finding is that *"depth is believable exactly when it describes ONE room — one ground, one light, one direction, every shadow explaining a distance"*, so three owners could drift from one another, which is the exact failure the vocabulary forbids. **The values graduated from EXP4 Study A (The Warm Layered Workspace), selected by ODL2 on 2026-07-17 — and selected on LAW, not on taste.** Studies B and C set type directly on the orchard (their headings, reminders and list rows sit on the landscape in their own screenshots), and Blueprint § 6.1 gives type ground beneath it *"without negotiation"*; § 4 now says the same. EXP4 itself judged C *"one step too little — support needs an anchor"*. A was the only study with a ground plane, which is the vocabulary's central member. **B and C were DELETED in the same change** (§ 17, retire on introduction), with their routes and their capture-harness entries. **Dark mode is completely resolved** (§ 16 forbids a partial mode): every warm shadow resolves to `none` rather than to a dimmer warm shadow, because the vocabulary IS a morning sun and at night there is no sun — a warm shadow at midnight is a lie about where the light comes from, and § 4 admits depth only to describe space truthfully. Rank is carried at night by tint and border: the same hierarchy, a different instrument. Study A had independently reached that answer. This closes Blueprint § 18 open item 4 for this vocabulary. **The ambient light pool declares a ceiling, not a pairing** (`--light-ambient-ceiling`), per the § 15 rule ODL2 added: a graded surface carrying no text has no colour pairing to measure, so it names the strength it may never exceed instead — which is what EXP4 asked for when it flagged its own radial pool as needing *"a named token with a stated ceiling"*.

**ADOPTED BY HOME'S E3 (NORTH1, 2026-07-17), and the reference is deleted.** This row's open migration is DISCHARGED, by the trigger it named rather than by anyone deciding it had waited long enough. `client/src/pages/home-experience-page.tsx` now stands on the ground plane, the warm shadows, the rim of light and the radius ladder, and it is a surface a household lands on. `pages/dev/material-a-warm-layers.tsx` and `scripts/capture-exp4-materiality-depth.ts` were deleted in that same change, which completes the disposition EXP4 § 6 set for all three studies: B and C lost the selection and died at ODL2, A won, graduated into UIA § 4, served as the vocabulary's reference implementation for exactly as long as it had no rival, and died the day a real room adopted it. No study outlived its own decision.

**NORTH2 (2026-07-17) — the values were RE-VALUED, and the law was not touched.** Every surface this row owns was `hsl(0 0% 100%)` — pure white, zero hue, zero saturation — in a room whose only light is a warm morning (`--light-rim: 48 60% 98%`). That is not a material; it is the absence of a decision, and it was the single strongest reason Home read as a beautiful web application rather than a room. No natural material is pure white: plaster, linen, oak and stone all carry hue and saturation, and a surface standing in warm light takes the colour of the light that falls on it. So: `--surface-primary` and `--card` → plaster `42 46% 98%`; `--surface-support` → linen over the counter, and MORE translucent (0.65 → 0.34) so the counter shows THROUGH the doors; `--ground-plane` → warmer stone at 0.82; `--surface-primary-border` → a joint rather than a drawn ring (7 lightness points off its fill → under 4). **The value RANGE narrowed deliberately** (canvas 95→94, card 100→98, saturation 27→46 RISING toward the light): planes are now read from the shadow beneath them and the rim of light along their top edge — which is how a real counter is read against a real wall — and never from a jump to a foreign colour. **`--shadow-support` INVERTED**: support was a drop-shadowed card floating ON the counter; it is now ETCHED INTO it (inset warm shadow at the top lip only — never four-sided, which is the disabled-input tell — plus a light rim on the lower lip, which is the one edge of a groove that faces the sun and the one line a disabled control never has). Hover lifts it out of the groove to meet the hand; press seats it back. **No law changed.** UIA §7 fixes the semantic STRUCTURE (one definition source, no raw colour in a surface, one meaning per colour) and every clause still holds — same named roles, same one place, and not one surface gained a colour of its own. §7 never fixed the VALUES, and the values were what was wrong. Authorised platform-wide by Colin Clapson (2026-07-17); scoping it to Home would have forked the one visual language UIA §17 forbids forking. **Verified beyond Home**: Planner, Cookbook, Pantry, Shopping and Dashboard captured at 1440×900 and inspected — no contrast or legibility regression (`docs/ui-audit/north2-home/rooms/`). Dark mode is a separate value set (§7) and is byte-untouched: it derives `--surface-primary` from its own `--card`, and its shadows were already `none`.

concerns.concern: Type roles (the named voices of the type scale)
concerns.owns:
The named type roles of **UIA § 8**'s scale — the classes a surface uses instead of picking a size and a weight. `.title-page` (32/38, 600) · `.title-section` (22/28, 600) · `.title-card` (16/22, 500) · `.text-table` (13/18) · `.text-numeric` (18/24, 600). A surface names the ROLE; the role names the numbers, once. This is UIA § 16's *"surfaces speak semantic only"* applied to type, and it is why a raw `text-[22px] font-semibold` in a surface is a defect.

**This row was created by NORTH3 (2026-07-17) and the owner it describes is not new — it is years old and had simply never been registered.** UIA § 17 requires every canonical building block to carry a visible register row, and five of THA's type roles did not have one; the sibling `.text-signature` (the third voice) has had a row since UXHOME1, so the scale was half-registered and nobody could see the gap. Creating this row **admits no new pattern and adds no law** — it records an owner that every surface in the product has been consuming all along. It is `review`, not `machine`: NORTH3 has not authored a machine check for it, and asserting one it had not validated would be worse than the silence it replaces.

**NORTH3 MOVED THESE ROLES FROM `@layer utilities` TO `@layer components`, AND THAT IS A CONTRACT CHANGE.** They were declared inside `@layer utilities` at index.css:593 — *after* `@tailwind utilities` at line 10. A role and a Tailwind utility are both single-class selectors (0,1,0), so specificity ties and **source order decided every contest: the role always won.** Any utility aimed at a role was dead on arrival, silently, with no error, no warning, and no way to see it except by measuring the rendered page.

**Two of Home's shipped, deliberate, carefully-argued intentions had already been killed by it, and both were discovered by measuring rather than by reading:**

1. **NORTH2's salutation.** It re-voiced "Welcome home," to `title-page font-normal` and wrote a paragraph explaining why the household's NAME must be the loudest thing in the room, quoting UIA § 8's own rule that *"shouting in bold is spending the emphasis budget on the shout"*. `.title-page`'s `font-weight: 600` beat `font-normal`. **The salutation shipped semibold — the exact thing the change was written to stop — and the comment describing the fix outlived the fix.**
2. **Home's signature.** It carries `leading-[1.02]` to pull the hand tight to the name. It measured **1.15** — `.text-signature`'s own line-height, to the decimal.

Both are now live and both were verified in the **compiled production CSS**, not merely in source: `.font-normal` at byte 70923 and `.leading-\[1\.02\]` at 71400 both fall after `.title-page` (18212) and `.text-signature` (18604). Measured in the browser: the salutation went 600 → **400**, and the signature's box went 101px → **90px** (88 × 1.02).

**The blast radius was measured before the move, and it is one surface.** A grep of every `title-page|title-section|title-card` in `client/src` for an adjacent font-weight or font-size utility returns exactly ONE hit — home-experience-page.tsx:576, NORTH2's `font-normal`. Nothing else in the codebase attempts to override a role, so nothing else can change when overriding starts working. Verified by looking as well: the five other rooms (planner · cookbook · pantry · shopping · dashboard) were captured before and after and are **byte-identical**, except the dashboard, which was proven by isolation to have drifted from the concurrent CONV1 P9 session's Stories-engine edits and **not** from this change — with the CSS reverted the dashboard still differed from its baseline, and with the CSS applied versus reverted it was byte-identical.

**What did NOT move:** `.scrollbar-hide`, `.text-premium` and `.calm-table` stayed in `@layer utilities`, because they are genuine utilities and component styles respectively. Only the six roles moved (the five here plus `.text-signature`, which keeps its own row), because only they are roles.

**The rule this row exists to carry:** *a role is a starting point, not a cage.* A surface that names a role and then adjusts one property of it is using the scale correctly, and it must be able to. If a role ever needs to be un-overridable, that is a decision to state out loud in this register — never a side-effect of which `@layer` block someone happened to paste it into.
